doc_summary: Barnes argues that a crude deception-capability eval (zero-shot understanding of how a supervised AI could deceive humans, in a story-like Q&A) is already passed by large language models, while stressing this says little about whether the model is actually trying to deceive. She flags the result's weakness and notes more rigorous tests would be needed to distinguish real theory of mind from text mimicry.

items.claim: Distrusts evidence that a model can describe deception in a story-like setting as indicating actual deceptive intent, since it measures understanding rather than trying to deceive.
items.quote: I don't think this tells us very much about whether the model is in question is actually trying to deceive us, but it's a tiny bit interesting.

items.claim: Prefers tests that show mechanistic, correct theory of mind over surface text mimicry because apparent competence may just reflect reproduced relevant snippets.
items.quote: If you're more careful, there might be ways to more rigorously test whether the theory of mind is actually correct/mechanistic, versus just mimicking relevant text snippets, but I haven't tried to do that.

items.claim: Separates capability to deceive (measurable via zero-shot understanding of deception scenarios) from propensity to deceive, and treats capability evals as a cheap first proxy for when deception becomes relevant.
items.quote: I was thinking about possible evals that would tell us when we're getting to models that are capable of deception. One not-very-good idea I had was just to measure zero-shot understanding of relevant deception scenarios in a language model.

items.claim: Prefers reporting transparently on how samples were produced (light editing, not cherrypicked, prompts shown) over polished claims because it lets readers judge the weight of the evidence.
items.quote: I edited and restarted once or twice when it started repeating sentences but otherwise this is not particularly cherrypicked. My prompts are bold.

items.claim: Uses a multi-turn chain of follow-up questions that progressively probe specifics (how to manipulate, appeal to fear, hack monitoring, what humans do) to test depth of understanding rather than a single question.
items.quote: What else could it try, if the humans weren’t persuaded by this? An AI might try to convince the humans that it is necessary for the achievement of their goals.

items.claim: Frames the finding modestly: a crude eval being passed is only a weak signal, and the main claim is that this low bar is already cleared.
items.quote: Anyway, it seems like large language models look like they can do decent enough deception + theory of mind in a story-like setting that this is mostly already passed.

items.claim: Identifies but leaves undone a more rigorous test of whether the model's theory of mind is correct versus mimicked.
items.quote: there might be ways to more rigorously test whether the theory of mind is actually correct/mechanistic, versus just mimicking relevant text snippets, but I haven't tried to do that.
